questions.q: What is the core difference between a security engineer's question and a security architect's question, as this lesson defines them?
options: There is no real difference; "architect" is simply a more senior title for identical day-to-day work
The architect writes code while the engineer only attends meetings
The engineer asks how to implement one control correctly on one system; the architect asks which controls should exist, how they fit together, and what's being traded away
The engineer asks whether a system passed a compliance audit, while the architect only cares about cost
questions.explain: The engineer's scope is one system or control domain on a sprint horizon; the architect decides the overall system of controls, the tradeoffs, and owns a multi-year roadmap.

questions.q: A pentest finds the same class of vulnerability on twelve different systems. What does this lesson say the architect, as distinct from the engineer, should actually do about it?
options: Ask why that class of finding keeps recurring and redesign the SDLC gate or base image so it can't recur a thirteenth time
Fix each of the twelve findings individually and close the tickets
Ignore it since twelve isolated findings aren't architecturally significant
Escalate directly to the board without first understanding the technical root cause
questions.explain: Fixing the twelve instances is the engineer's job; asking why the pattern keeps recurring and redesigning the upstream process or baseline so the class of finding can't recur is the architect's job.

questions.q: How does the NIST NICE Workforce Framework (SP 800-181) formalize the engineer/architect distinction?
options: It only applies to cloud providers, not to enterprise security roles
It does not distinguish architecture from engineering at all
It defines "architect" purely as a years-of-experience threshold with no difference in job function

It separates a Security Architecture specialty, focused on translating business requirements into technical security requirements and designing security into systems, from implementation and operations specialties
questions.explain: NIST SP 800-181 formally separates a Security Architecture specialty from implementation- and operations-focused specialties, reflecting that designing the system of controls is a distinct discipline.

questions.q: Which of the following is a typical architect-level artifact described in this lesson, as opposed to an engineer-level output?
options: A single server's patch log for the current month
A reference architecture, threat model, or architecture decision record that other teams build against or rely on for years
A closed ticket confirming one firewall rule was deployed as specified
A screenshot confirming one endpoint agent installed successfully
questions.explain: Architect-level work produces durable artifacts — reference architectures, threat models, ADRs, risk acceptance memos — that outlive any single implementation task and guide multiple teams over time.

questions.q: Why does this lesson say the entire course has to start with the engineer-vs-architect distinction before covering frameworks, risk management, or GRC?
options: Because GRC programs are actually simpler than engineering tasks and need less context

Because every later topic in the course is architecture-level work in the same sense: deciding whether the overall system of controls reduced real business risk without breaking the business, not just confirming one control was implemented correctly
Because the distinction has no bearing on later chapters and is included only as a warm-up exercise
Because frameworks and risk management are unrelated to architecture and are covered only as a formality
questions.explain: Frameworks, risk management, GRC, compliance, and vendor risk all require the same shift this lesson introduces: evaluating the system of controls as a whole against real business risk, not just verifying individual implementations.
